कुरुक्षेत्र। सावन माह की शुरुआत बारिश के साथ होने से लोगों को भीषण गर्मी और उमस से बड़ी राहत मिली। गुरुवार को दोपहर तक तेज धूप और उमस भरी गर्मी ने लोगों को बेहाल किए रखा, लेकिन शाम होते-होते मौसम ने करवट ली और झमाझम बारिश शुरू हो गई। बारिश के चलते तापमान में गिरावट दर्ज की गई और मौसम सुहावना हो गया। हालांकि कहीं तेज तो कहीं हल्की बारिश रही, जो 10 एमएम से अधिक दर्ज की गई। आज शुक्रवार को भी बारिश होने की संभावना है।
बारिश के कारण शहर के कई निचले इलाकों और प्रमुख मार्गों पर जलभराव भी हुआ। इससे वाहन चालकों और राहगीरों को परेशानी का सामना करना पड़ा। हालांकि, लंबे समय से गर्मी और उमस से परेशान लोगों ने बारिश का स्वागत किया और राहत की सांस ली। वहीं बारिश होने व अगले कुछ दिनों तक ऐसा ही मौसम बने रहने की संभावना से किसानों ने भी राहत महसूस की है। इसका धान की फसल पर साकारात्मक असर पड़ेगा।
अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 28 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। विभाग ने शुक्रवार को भी जिले में हल्की से मध्यम बारिश की संभावना जताई है। बागवानी विशेषज्ञ डॉ सीबी सिंह का कहना है कि बारिश का सिलसिला जारी रहने की उम्मीद है ।

दिन से ज्यादा गर्म हो रही हैं जम्मू-कश्मीर की रातें, IIT खड़गपुर की चेतावनी; सेब-ग्लेशियर और नदियों पर मंडराया खतरा
आईआईटी खड़गपुर के शोध के अनुसार, जम्मू-कश्मीर के पहाड़ी इलाकों में 20 वर्षों में तापमान 1 डिग्री सेल्सियस बढ़ा है। यह वृद्धि ग्लेशियरों, नदियों और कृष ...और पढ़ें

पिछले 20 वर्षों में तापमान 1 डिग्री सेल्सियस बढ़ा
ग्लेशियर पिघलने से नदियों, कृषि पर गंभीर खतरा
रात में और ऊंचाई पर तापमान तेजी से बढ़ रहा
डिजिटल डेस्क, जम्मू। पहाड़ी इलाको में तापमान बढ़ना खतरे की बात मानी जाती है। क्योंकि तापमान बढ़ने से न केवल प्राकृतिक स्थिती खराब होती बल्कि किसानों को भी भारी नुकसान होता है। जम्मू-कश्मीर के पहाड़ी इलाकों में तापमान में बढ़ोतरी देखी गई है। जिससे आने वाले समय को लेकर लोगों की चिंता बढ़ने लगी है।
IIT के वैज्ञानिकों ने जम्मू-कश्मीर के तापमान पर किया रिसर्च
हाल ही में आईआईटी खड़गपुर के वैज्ञानिकों द्वारा जम्मू-कश्मीर के बदलते तापमान पर एक रिसर्च किया गया। इस रिसर्च में पता चला कि पिछले 20 वर्षों में तापमान लगभग एक डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ा है।
यह अध्ययन भारतीय प्रौद्योगिकी संस्थान (आईआईटी) खड़गपुर के सेंटर फॉर ओसियन, रिवर, एटमॉस्फियर एंड लैंड साइंसेज (CORAL) के वैज्ञानिकों, प्रोफेसर जयनारायणन कुट्टिपुरथ, जी. एस. गोपीकृष्णन और वी. एम. प्रणव चंद्रन द्वारा किया गया। इस रिसर्च में कुछ अन्य महत्वपूर्ण बातें भी सामने आई।
इस अध्ययन में भारतीय मौसम विज्ञान विभाग (IMD) के जम्मू, कटड़ा, बटोट, भद्रवाह, बनिहाल, काजीगुंड, श्रीनगर, पहलगाम, गुलमर्ग और कुपवाड़ा स्थित दस मौसम केंद्रों के तापमान आंकड़ों का विश्लेषण किया गया।
कुछ महत्वपूर्ण बातें जो रिसर्च में मिली
जम्मू-कश्मीर में तापमान में हो रही वृद्धि सभी क्षेत्रों में बराबर नहीं है। मध्य और अधिक ऊंचाई वाले पर्वतीय क्षेत्रों में तापमान मैदानी इलाकों की अपेक्षा अधिक तेजी से बढ़ रहा है। इस प्रक्रिया को एलिवेशन-डिपेंडेंट वार्मिंग कहा जाता है। इसका मतलब है कि जैसे-जैसे ऊंचाई बढ़ती है, जलवायु परिवर्तन का प्रभाव भी अधिक स्पष्ट दिखाई देता है।
खबरें और भी
तापमान दिन के मुकाबले रात में ज्यादा बढ़ रहा है। कई पर्वतीय मौसम केंद्रों पर न्यूनतम तापमान प्रति दशक 0.1 से 0.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ा है। वैज्ञानिकों का मानना है कि वातावरण में बढ़ती नमी रात के समय पृथ्वी से निकलने वाली ऊष्मा को रोक लेती है, जिससे रातें पहले की तुलना में अधिक गर्म हो रही हैं।
ठंड के मौसम में तापमान वृद्धि सबसे अधिक देखी गई है। इसका मुख्य कारण बर्फ की मात्रा में कमी और पृथ्वी की सतह की रिफलेक्टेंस यानी परावर्तन क्षमता (अल्बीडो) में बदलाव माना गया है। जब बर्फ कम होती है तो गहरी सतह अधिक सौर्य ऊर्जा अवशोषित (ऑब्जर्व) करती है, जिससे तापमान और बढ़ जाता है।
तापमान बढ़ने से होगा नुकसान
जम्मू-कश्मीर के अधिकांश ग्लेशियर बर्फ के लगातार जमा होने और कम तापमान पर निर्भर करते हैं। अगर ग्लेशियरस तेजी से पिघलने लगे तो भविष्य में नेचुर्ल वॉटर की मात्रा कम हो जाएगी।
जम्मू-कश्मीर की कई नदियां, जैसे झेलम, चिनाब और सिंध, ग्लेशियरों और बर्फ के पिघलने से मिलने वाले पानी पर निर्भर हैं। शुरुआत में अधिक पिघलाव से नदियों में पानी बढ़ सकता है, लेकिन जब ग्लेशियर छोटे होने लगेंगे, तो गर्मियों में नदियों में पानी कम हो सकता है। इससे आने वाले समय में शिचीईं और अन्य काम प्रभावित होंगे।
अगर तापमान ऐसे ही बढ़ता रहा तो जम्मू-कश्मीर में उगने वाले पहाड़ी फलों का भी नुकसान होगा। सेब, अखरोट और चेरी जैसी फसलों को सर्दियों में निश्चित ठंड (chilling hours) की आवश्यकता होती है। तापमान बढ़ने पर इनकी गुणवत्ता और उत्पादन प्रभावित हो सकता है। कीट और बीमारियों का खतरा बढ़ सकता है। खेती के मौसम और फसल चक्र में बदलाव आ सकता है।
इसके साथ ही पहलगाम और गुलमर्ग जैसे ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में पिछले लगभग 20 वर्षों में तापमान लगभग एक डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ चुका है। यह पश्चिमी हिमालय में तेजी से हो रहे जलवायु परिवर्तन का संकेत है। वैज्ञानिकों ने बताया कि तीन हजार मीटर से अधिक ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में लॉन्ग टर्म डेटा सीमित है। इसका भविष्य में ज्यादा सही अध्ययन करने के लिए अधिक वेदर स्टेशन स्थापित करने की आवश्यकता है।

articles.full_text:
Coal demand and prices in China have jumped in recent days as scorching heat waves across most of the country boost electricity demand.
The benchmark spot coal prices at the port of Qinhuangdao have erased a slump from earlier this month and are on track for further increases in the coming weeks amid intense heat, according to the China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association.
“Thermal coal prices are more likely to rise than fall, as the peak season for coal-fired power consumption is far from over, the impacts of El Niño have yet to fully materialize, and the cumulative effects of tightening supply and growing demand will continue to build,” Li Xuegang, a senior analyst at the association, said on a webcast carried by Bloomberg.
China’s spot thermal coal prices are also being lifted by new mine shutdowns in the top coal-producing province, according to analysts at Mysteel.
“Market sentiment jumped amid renewed supply concerns after four coal mines in Yulin, the largest producing hub in Northwest China's Shaanxi province, were ordered to suspend operations the same day,” Mysteel analysts wrote.
“This could provide a fresh catalyst for a market that has already begun to show signs of strengthening.”
Most of central and eastern China are in the grip of high summer temperatures, while northeastern China, including the large cities of Beijing and Shenyang, is expected to see unusually high temperatures into this weekend.
Heat waves are also depressing hydropower output and wind power generation, which China will have to partly offset with increased coal consumption.
China’s coal inventories are sufficiently high, but its domestic production has seen setbacks since the deadliest mining disaster in 16 years in May prompted authorities to step up safety checks and order suspension of activities in a number of mines in the Shanxi region.
Chinese authorities are not restricting coal power growth in the new five-year energy plan as Beijing doubles down on the fossil fuel as a “bottom-line guarantee” of the electricity system amid rising shares of renewable power.
By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

Netherlands has had six days of "extreme heat" above 35 degrees this year
The Netherlands recorded its sixth regional "extreme heat day" of the year after temperatures climbed past 35°C on Wednesday, placing 2026 within striking distance of the all-time national record.
By meteorological definition in the Netherlands, a regional extreme heat day is triggered as soon as at least one official weather station in the country clocks a temperature of 35.0°C or higher. Wednesday marked the sixth day this year to hit this extreme threshold. The five previous 35°C+ days occurred in rapid succession earlier this summer on June 19, 24, 25, 26, and 27.
The 35°C mark was breached across six different national weather stations simultaneously, including Westdorpe and Gilze-Rijen, which both hit a peak of 35.2°C, alongside Maastricht, Volkel, Eindhoven, and Woensdrecht.
This current streak places this summer at the absolute upper echelon of Dutch climate history. With 6 extreme heat days, this year has officially tied the runner-up record set in 2003. It is now just one day away from tying the all-time historic record of 7 days, which was established during the relentless heatwaves of 2020.
While July 29 hovered just above 35°C, it did not surpass the highest temperature of 2026, which remains the 39.4°C recorded in the village of Ell on June 26.
Even though the absolute national maximum record wasn't shattered on Wednesday, local and date-specific milestones were heavily rewritten. The primary Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) station in De Bilt reached 31.7°C (peaking eventually at 32.8°C regionally), entirely breaking the previous July 29 date record of 31.5°C that had stood since 1948.
Meteorologists from Weeronline emphasize that this milestone highlights a severe, rapid acceleration of climate change. In the early 20th century, a 35°C day anywhere in the Netherlands was a generational anomaly, occurring roughly once every 15 years.
Due to modern warming trends, the frequency has expanded exponentially to an average of once every 1.5 years, with extreme summers like this one compressing multiple occurrences into just a matter of weeks.
The intense multi-day pressure cooker is finally breaking. A cooler westerly wind is moving across the country today, pushing temperatures down significantly to a more comfortable 22°C to 27°C heading into the weekend.

Extreme heat threatens Nepal’s economy as warming accelerates
A new World Bank report warns Nepal is warming faster than most South Asian countries, with heatwaves increasingly hurting workers, straining infrastructure and putting economic growth at risk.In the scorching mid-June afternoon, as temperatures hovered around 40 degrees Celsius, 67-year-old Gopal Damai was still pulling his rickshaw through the streets of Mahendranagar in far-western Nepal.
For four decades, he has earned his living transporting goods in the three-wheeled cart. But increasingly frequent and intense heatwaves have made that livelihood harder to sustain.
“I only work in the morning and evening. I can't work during the day,” he told Kantipur Daily in May.
“Some days, I don't even earn Rs100. I have to buy vegetables on credit.”
The blistering heat has emptied Mahendranagar's streets. Fewer people venture outdoors during the day, leaving Damai with few customers and even fewer opportunities to earn.
More than 250 kilometres east, in Bardiya's Gulariya Municipality, 37-year-old Puja Bhujuwa faces a similar struggle.
She spends long hours pushing a cart and selling roasted corn near the district land revenue office.
The heat radiating from the asphalt burns her feet, while the 40-degree temperature leaves her with persistent headaches. Despite the oppressive conditions, she must keep roasting corn over a wood fire to support her family.
“Business was good until April,”Bhujuwa told Kantipur in May. “Since June, the heat has intensified, people have stopped coming out during the day, and our sales have dropped sharply.”
The hardships faced by Damai and Bhujuwa illustrate a broader trend.
Extreme heat is no longer confined to Nepal's southern Tarai. Hill towns and cities, including the Kathmandu Valley, are also experiencing steadily rising temperatures, exposing millions of workers to growing health and economic risks.
In Kathmandu, the heat is increasingly taking a toll on informal and daily wage workers who spend long hours outdoors, often without access to shade, cooling facilities or adequate drinking water.
Nepal, long regarded as a cool Himalayan country, is now emerging as one of South Asia's fastest-warming nations, according to the World Bank's 2026 report, A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities.
The report says Nepal has already warmed by 1.26 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, making it one of the region's fastest-warming countries. Under a medium-emissions scenario, temperatures are projected to rise by another 2.8 degrees Celsius by the end of the century.
The warming will be most pronounced across the Himalayas and foothills, where rising temperatures are expected to alter regional weather patterns, increase humidity and intensify heat across the Indo-Gangetic plains.
Urban centres in Nepal's hills are also warming rapidly. Kathmandu already experiences a pronounced urban heat island effect, with temperatures in the city core reaching up to 4 degrees Celsius higher than surrounding parts of the valley because of dense construction, concrete surfaces and shrinking green spaces.
Although Kathmandu still experiences fewer days of extreme heat than many lowland South Asian cities, the report warns that warming trends indicate even high-altitude cities will increasingly face dangerous heat stress.
Between May 2024 and May 2025, Nepal recorded 89 days with temperatures above the historical 90th percentile, underscoring how quickly extreme heat is becoming the new normal.
According to the World Bank, extreme heat is steadily eroding Nepal's economic productivity by reducing workers' capacity to perform physically demanding jobs, particularly in construction, agriculture and the informal sector. Rising temperatures are also increasing electricity demand, overheating buildings and disrupting transport systems.
Poor households are expected to bear the heaviest burden. Families living in informal settlements often lack reliable electricity, cooling facilities and access to healthcare, making them especially vulnerable to prolonged heatwaves.
The report estimates that more than 700 million people across India, Bangladesh and Nepal already live in areas where outdoor heat stress exceeds safe physiological limits for at least one day every year.
The health burden is also rising rapidly across the region. Across Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka, deaths in which high temperatures were identified as a contributing risk factor nearly doubled between 2000 and 2023—from around 118,000 to approximately 230,000—representing an increase of about 95 percent, or an average annual rise of 4.1 percent.
The report also calls for stronger monitoring of heat-related illnesses and deaths, expanded early warning systems, greener urban planning and the adoption of heat-resilient building standards.
According to the report, embedding heat resilience into urban planning, infrastructure investment and public health systems before temperatures rise further could prevent extreme heat from becoming a long-term constraint on Nepal's economic growth and livability.
The report explains that the human body maintains an internal temperature of about 37 degrees Celsius. Physical activity generates heat, while sweating and the widening of blood vessels near the skin help cool the body. But hotter air, higher humidity and prolonged exposure to direct sunlight or heated surfaces reduce the body's ability to dissipate heat.
When those natural cooling mechanisms fail, people become vulnerable to heat exhaustion, heatstroke and other illnesses that place severe stress on the heart, lungs and kidneys, sometimes resulting in death.
Beyond the health risks, the World Bank warns that extreme heat is already weighing heavily on South Asia's economy.
The equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs are lost annually across the region as workers slow down, stop work early or fall ill. Businesses also suffer as electricity systems, transport networks and buildings struggle to function efficiently under extreme temperatures, reducing productivity, investment and economic output.
According to the report, informal workers' incomes decline by about 40 percent during a heatwave. At the same time, household spending on drinking water, cooling and healthcare rises sharply. Prolonged heat can also force families to borrow money, sell productive assets or pull children out of school to cope with financial stress.
Without adequate adaptation measures, rising temperatures could reduce South Asia's gross domestic product by nearly 7 percent by 2050, the steepest projected decline among developing regions. Shrinking tax revenues coupled with rising public spending on healthcare, energy and damaged infrastructure could create a prolonged fiscal burden for governments.
Dr Prajal Pradhan, associate professor at the Integrated Research on Energy, Environment and Society at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, said intensifying heatwaves would affect Nepal through both public health and the economy.
“Heatwaves worsen existing illnesses, increase heat-related deaths and reduce labour productivity,” he said.
“As heatwaves become more frequent, demand for cooling will increase, and this requires more electricity. Poor ventilation in buildings also leads to overheating as temperatures rise. Extreme heat can even soften asphalt and disrupt transport systems.”
Pradhan said households living in poorly constructed homes remain highly vulnerable to both cold spells and heatwaves.
“The long-term solution is to ensure decent housing with proper heating and cooling facilities. Expanding green spaces and water bodies in urban areas can also help reduce temperatures and lessen the impact of heatwaves.”
The report said that dense urban areas can remain more than 10 degrees Celsius warmer than surrounding rural areas at night because concrete and asphalt retain heat long after sunset. The lack of nighttime cooling prevents the human body from recovering from daytime heat stress, making prolonged heat exposure even more dangerous.
By 2070, around 520 million people across South Asia are projected to experience at least one month of dangerous heat every year—four times the current number. Much of that exposure will be concentrated in cities, while the Himalayas and their foothills are expected to experience the fastest rate of warming.
The report also warns that the true death toll from extreme heat is likely far higher than official figures indicate because many fatalities are recorded as cardiac or kidney failure rather than heat-related deaths.
Economist Chandra Mani Adhikari said extreme heat is already affecting multiple sectors of Nepal's economy.
“Heatwaves have not only reduced agricultural production but have also significantly affected public health and employment,”he said. “Government and household healthcare spending has risen considerably, while disasters linked to climate change are damaging critical infrastructure.” According to Adhikari, Nepal has failed to adequately strengthen its climate adaptation programmes.
“The current trend suggests Nepal could face growing food insecurity if these problems are not properly analysed and addressed,” he said.
To reduce future losses, the World Bank proposes a broad set of interventions spanning public health, social protection, energy, transport, finance and urban planning.
It recommends investing in early warning systems, strengthening health services, protecting outdoor workers, expanding urban forests and shaded public spaces, and making electricity and transport systems more resilient to extreme heat.
“Heatwaves disrupt every part of city life, so the response must involve the whole of government,” the report says. It also calls for mobilising private investment to expand access to affordable cooling, finance green and climate-resilient buildings, improve cooling systems for industry and healthcare, and develop insurance mechanisms to manage heat-related risks.
Rather than creating entirely new programmes, the report recommends integrating heat resilience into existing initiatives. Employment schemes such as Nepal's National Employment Promotion Programme, national health systems and housing programmes could incorporate heat adaptation measures by updating operational guidelines without requiring major new spending.
The report also highlights the role of frontline community workers. Nepal's Female Community Health Volunteers could help deliver heat advisories and protect pregnant women, children and elderly people through the systems already in place.
As air-conditioning becomes more common, electricity demand is expected to shift increasingly to the evening and night because buildings retain heat after sunset and nighttime temperatures are rising faster than daytime temperatures.
The tourism sector is also expected to face growing risks.
The report recommends retrofitting heritage sites in the Kathmandu Valley—including the Durbar Squares, Pashupatinath, Bauddhanath and Swayambhunath—as well as lowland pilgrimage destinations such as Lumbini and Janakpur with shaded walkways, water features, traditional courtyard ventilation and cool-roof technologies that comply with conservation standards.
According to the report, the Nepal Tourism Board, the Department of Archaeology, UNESCO, the Asian Development Bank and private investors could jointly finance these improvements to protect tourism assets that support an industry worth around $700 million and provide employment for nearly one million people.
The report also recommends strengthening Nepal's electricity network through grid upgrades, distributed renewable energy with battery storage, demand-side management and priority power supply for critical services during periods of extreme heat.
Low-cost interventions such as shaded bus stops, cooler pavements, tree-lined streets and improved pedestrian and cycling infrastructure could also reduce heat exposure, particularly in the Tarai and Kathmandu Valley, according to the report.

Newsroom
The scorching temperatures gripping Cyprus aren't just making people uncomfortable; they're also sending more of them to the hospital.
Public hospital emergency departments are reporting a noticeable increase in patients as the island continues to bake under the recent heatwave, with doctors treating everything from dehydration and heat exhaustion to twisted ankles and food poisoning.
According to Charalambos Charilaou, spokesperson for the State Health Services Organisation (OKYpY), emergency departments have seen a rise in both patient visits and hospital admissions in recent days.
Part of the increase is seasonal.
With more people heading to the beaches, hiking trails, and holiday destinations, coastal towns are seeing a surge in visitors, while the influx of tourists is also adding pressure to emergency services.
"The high temperatures, combined with outdoor activities at the sea and in the mountains, are leading to more people seeking medical attention," Charilaou said.
The most common cases include heat exhaustion, dehydration, cuts and injuries from slipping on rocks, sprained ankles, and other minor limb injuries.
Doctors are also seeing more cases of gastroenteritis, a common summer illness often linked to food that has spoiled in the heat.
Charilaou warned that food and drinks can quickly become unsafe if they are not stored at the correct temperature, increasing the risk of stomach bugs and gastrointestinal problems.
While patients of all ages are turning up at emergency departments, hospitals say the people most at risk remain young children, older adults, and those with heart or lung conditions, who can become seriously unwell much faster in extreme heat.
Health officials are urging people not to underestimate the temperatures.
Their advice is simple: stay indoors or in the shade during the hottest hours of the day, use air conditioning where possible, drink plenty of water to replace fluids lost through sweating, and wear light, loose-fitting clothing.
The warning comes as Cyprus continues to experience another intense summer, with prolonged periods of extreme heat placing increasing pressure not only on the electricity grid but also on the island's healthcare system.

HYDERABAD: Telangana received widespread rainfall over the last few days after a prolonged rain deficit, bringing relief to farmers, news agency PTI reported.
Gullakota in Jagtial district received 70.5mm of rainfall till noon on Thursday, followed by 66.6mm at Sirpur (U) in Kumuram Bheem Asifabad district, according to the Telangana Development Planning Society.
The state's rainfall deficit, which stood at 33% 15 days ago, had narrowed to 10% by Thursday morning, according to the India Meteorological Department (
IMD).
However, 13 of Telangana's 33 districts have received less than 20% of their normal rainfall so far.
The rainfall deficit in Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri district remains as high as 65%, while rainfall continues to be below normal in Hyderabad as well, PTI reported.
The rains caused waterlogging and traffic snarls at several places in Hyderabad on the night of July 29. Rivulets were also in spate at some places across the state following the showers, disrupting normal life.
In its weather warning, the IMD issued a 'red alert' for isolated places in Adilabad, Kumuram Bheem Asifabad, Mancherial, Nirmal and Jagtial districts. It forecast very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall accompanied by strong surface winds from 1pm on Thursday to 8.30am on July 31.
The IMD said light to moderate rain or thundershowers are likely at most places over Telangana during the same period.
A 'red alert' indicates extremely heavy rainfall of over 204mm in 24 hours.
In view of the forecast for moderate to heavy rainfall, the Cyberabad Traffic Police, in an advisory, asked companies, including IT firms and organisations operating in the area to consider work from home wherever possible.
It also advised organisations to follow staggered early logouts from 2pm onwards to minimise travel-related risks, ease pressure on road infrastructure and ensure the smooth functioning of essential services amid adverse weather conditions.
In a post on 'X', the Cyberabad Traffic Police said the advisory was issued keeping in mind public safety, productivity, the possibility of severe traffic congestion and the need to ensure uninterrupted emergency services, PTI reported.
(With agency inputs)

The Ahmedabad Rural Police have cancelled all personnel leave, activated emergency response systems and intensified surveillance across the district after the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for heavy rainfall on July 31 and August 1.
Addressing the media on Thursday, Ahmedabad Rural Superintendent of Police Om Prakash Jat said all police stations and traffic personnel had been placed on high alert, with district control rooms functioning round the clock to respond swiftly to rain-related emergencies.
"As part of our preparedness, all police stations and traffic staff have been deployed for continuous patrolling and monitoring. District control rooms are fully operational and emergency response mechanisms have been activated," Jat said.
Police Issue Travel Advisory
The Ahmedabad Rural Police have advised motorists to avoid non-essential travel during periods of heavy rainfall, particularly on roads and highways prone to waterlogging.
In a separate traffic advisory, commuters travelling on the Sanathal-Bavla Highway have been urged to exercise extreme caution, maintain safe speeds, keep adequate distance from other vehicles and avoid crossing flooded stretches where water levels appear unsafe.
Police have also advised travellers to check the latest weather and traffic updates before commencing their journeys.
Disaster Response Teams on Standby
Police teams have been deployed in villages that witnessed flooding during previous spells of heavy rain, with officers monitoring vulnerable areas continuously.
To strengthen disaster preparedness, two State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams have been stationed at Bavla and Viramgam, while a National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) team has been deployed at Dholka for immediate rescue and relief operations, if required.
The district administration is also setting up village-wise relief shelters to accommodate residents who may need to be evacuated from low-lying areas.
Industries, Residents Asked to Coordinate With Police
The Superintendent of Police appealed to industries across Ahmedabad Rural to relocate workers to safer locations in advance wherever necessary and coordinate with the police to facilitate safe movement.
Residents of flood-prone areas, including Bopal, Sanand and neighbouring localities, who plan to temporarily shift to safer places have also been requested to inform the nearest police station. Police said this would enable officers to keep watch over locked houses and help protect residents' property during their absence.
Jat urged residents to remain vigilant, avoid panic buying or hoarding of essential commodities, rely only on official updates issued by government agencies, and dial the 112 emergency helpline in the event of any emergency.

Depression over Central India to keep Telangana under wet spell; IMD issues red alert for 5 districts
The weather system is expected to move westwards while gradually weakening into a depression over the next 12 to 24 hours but is likely to continue influencing weather over Telangana
By - Newsmeter Network |Representative Image
Hyderabad: Telangana is set for another spell of widespread rain.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said a deep depression over West-Central Chhattisgarh and adjoining Vidarbha and Southeast Madhya Pradesh, coupled with a vigorous southwest monsoon, is driving heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across the State.
The weather system is expected to move westwards while gradually weakening into a depression over the next 12 to 24 hours but is likely to continue influencing weather over Telangana.
Alerts sounded for 5 districts
The IMD has issued a Red Alert for Adilabad, Komaram Bheem Asifabad, Mancherial, Nirmal and Jagtial districts, where very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall accompanied by strong surface winds of 40-50 kmph is likely at isolated places on Thursday.
An Orange Alert has been sounded for Nizamabad, Rajanna Sircilla, Karimnagar, Peddapalli, Jayashankar Bhupalpally, Mulugu and Kamareddy districts, where heavy to very heavy rainfall with gusty winds is expected.
A Yellow Alert has been issued for Hyderabad, Medchal-Malkajgiri, Rangareddy, Sangareddy, Medak, Siddipet, Vikarabad, Hanamkonda, Warangal, Mahabubabad, Bhadradri Kothagudem and Jangaon, where heavy rain is likely at isolated places.
Hyderabad likely to witness moderate to heavy rain
For Hyderabad, the IMD has forecast a generally cloudy sky with moderate to heavy rain or thundershowers accompanied by strong surface winds of 30-40 kmph during the next 24 hours.
Day temperatures are expected to remain around 27°C, while the minimum temperature is likely to be 23°C. During the following 48 hours, the city is likely to receive light to moderate rain or thundershowers in parts of the city, with the maximum temperature rising to around 32°C.
At 8:30 am on Thursday, Hyderabad recorded a maximum temperature of 26°C, a minimum of 23.2°C, relative humidity of 97 per cent and rainfall of 10.8 mm.
Rain eases after Friday
According to the IMD forecast, light to moderate rain or thundershowers are likely at most places across Telangana on Thursday and at many places on Friday.
Rainfall activity is expected to reduce from August 1, with showers confined to a few places, and thereafter only isolated places until August 5. However, strong surface winds of 30-40 kmph are expected to continue across all districts until August 5, even as rainfall intensity decreases.
Heavy rain already widespread in many districts
The IMD said very heavy rainfall was recorded at many places in Komaram Bheem Asifabad, at a few places in Mancherial and Jayashankar Bhupalpally, and at isolated places in Adilabad, Jagtial, Mulugu and Peddapalli. Heavy rainfall was also reported from several other northern districts, with the southwest monsoon remaining vigorous over Telangana.
Public advisory
With heavy rain and gusty winds expected, residents have been advised to:
- Avoid travelling through waterlogged roads unless essential.
- Stay away from low-lying areas prone to flooding.
- Avoid taking shelter under trees or near electricity poles during thunderstorms.
- Secure loose outdoor objects due to strong winds.
- Follow official advisories issued by the IMD and district authorities.

articles.full_text: India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for Mumbai on Thursday, forecasting thunderstorms with lightning, heavy rainfall at isolated places and gusty winds. Thane and Raigad have been placed under an orange alert for heavy to very heavy rainfall. Mumbai will remain under a yellow alert on Friday (July 31), with heavy rain and strong winds also expected.
